prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock, based on trapping many atoms at a magic wavelength, and its development to the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: After the full first round I keep the lattice clock as my single preferred part, and I tested it again against the chair's point that our opening rankings may have driven the convergence. On the evidence, the discovery is an original invention: the magic-wavelength condition makes the light shift equal for both clock states, so thousands of atoms can be held without Doppler or recoil shifts while the clock transition is undisturbed. That idea is not a better comb and not a better ion trap, and it is what made 10^-18 reachable. It has been experimentally verified and compared across independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST), which is the test I care about most. It also gives a new window: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift is already measured in the laboratory. The credit is compact. Katori proposed the lattice and made the first strontium demonstrations; Ye's group took the clock to the accuracy and stability frontier and developed the many-body and comb-linked clock physics. I would defend the two-name credit in the citation by saying plainly that it rests on the invention and its first realisation plus the demonstrated frontier performance, not on who holds the current record. I would not add a third name or a second part. Nothing in the first round supplied primary-literature evidence for a third claimant of the same weight.
statement.case_against: The unresolved weaknesses are the same three, and I do not think the round-1 exchange removed them. First, novelty against 2005 (combs) and 2012 (control of single quantum systems, including ion clocks): the committee must be able to say why the lattice clock is a distinct idea, not a successor step. Second, the fundamental-physics payoff is so far a set of bounds and null results, not a deviation from known physics. Danielsson's condition is fair, and I read the record as modest but real bounds, with the strongest result being the redshift measurement, not a new law. A prize for discovery should not lean on that payoff. It must rest on the invention and the verified new regime. Third, Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Derevianko and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups, and the Al+ ion-clock tradition, have real claims that a two-name credit cannot absorb. I rely partly on memory for the priority details, and the committee should have the expert reports confirm them before the vote.

responses.point: Danielsson moved the lattice clock to the head of his list but conditions his support on competitive physics bounds on constants, dark matter or gravity, and calls the instrument an invention more than a discovery about nature.
responses.response: I agree the condition is the right one to state openly. My answer is that the discovery here is the demonstrated ability to read out a clean quantum system at 10^-18, and the millimetre redshift measurement and the existing constraints show that this is already physics and not only metrology. I would not want the citation to claim a fundamental result that has not been found. So I would keep the citation on the invention and the accuracy regime, and record in the committee statement that the bounds on constants and dark matter are real but not yet decisive. If the expert reports show that those bounds are not competitive with other methods, I would still support the prize, because the criterion is an original, verified invention that opens a door. I would not support it if the case needed a null result to be read as a discovery.

responses.point: Mehlig keeps B007 first, admits that the omission of Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Fu is the real weak point, and asks whether lattice clocks should take precedence in a one-prize year; he lists B042 as his fallback.
responses.response: I think he has the weak point right, and it is the reason I cannot move to B007. The Kane-Mele proposal and Molenkamp's HgTe experiment are the right pair, but the HgTe route was proposed by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and the 3D story belongs to Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore and Hasan. I want the credited people to be those who did the original work, and a three-name set leaves a serious claim outside, plus part of the conceptual ground overlaps with 2016. Mehlig has said B042 is his fallback and that he checked the physics, and I welcome that. I would ask him whether a Z2 prize could ever be drawn to a citation that is safe against the HgTe-proposal objection, and if he cannot show that, I hope he can join B042 in the final vote. I would keep B007 under review for another year.

responses.point: Eriksson keeps twisted bilayer graphene first with MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, and asks whether a maturity argument undervalues the speed of confirmation by many independent groups.
responses.response: The speed of independent confirmation is a real point and I do not want to dismiss it. I ranked B054 third because the prediction and the 2018 experiments are a strong theory-plus-experiment story. My concern remains that the pairing mechanism is open and twist-angle disorder limits how sure we are that the phases are intrinsic. Experimental reproduction tells us that the phases are there, but not yet what the stable, citable discovery is. His two-name version is the cleaner credit, and he has been honest that Cao and Fatemi, the experimental first authors, are left out by the three-laureate and group-leader convention. I would record that in the statement. I keep B054 as my first alternative, and I would not object to a future prize, but I would not choose it over a verified and consolidated result this year.

responses.point: Lindroth separates breadth of support from merit, checked B042 on its own terms, and says a lattice clock turned the comb into a standard better than caesium by orders of magnitude and is not incremental.
responses.response: I agree with her method and with the main step, but I would refine the wording of the argument. The comb makes optical frequencies countable and the lattice clock is what supplies a better reference to count, so the two prizes cover related but distinct steps, and I think the citation should say that the lattice and magic wavelength are the point. I would not accept 'better than caesium by orders of magnitude' as the sole basis for the credit, because that is the later-and-better-experiment argument I worry about for Ye. I would rather the citation mention the lattice concept first and the accuracy second. She and Johansson also defer to each other on B056, and I accept that: on the evidence in this room, I do not press B056 above the clock.

responses.point: Kroll wants the citation to state explicitly why Katori and Ye are named, and notes that the Hall laboratory and JILA connection is his disclosed link to Ye's environment.
responses.response: I agree and I would go further and put it in writing for the committee record, not only in the citation. The record should say that Katori is credited for the proposal and first realisation of the magic-wavelength lattice clock and Ye for demonstrating it at the accuracy and stability frontier, with the many-body and comb-linked clock work. It should say that PTB, SYRTE, NIST, Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Derevianko are not credited because the three-laureate limit and the original-work criterion lead to the group that proposed and the group that took it to the frontier. On his Hall-laboratory link, I see a collegial history without a joint publication with Ye or Katori, and I do not think it needs more handling than a note.

uncertainties: Whether the expert reports confirm the priority record for Katori and Ye against Lemonde, Derevianko, Takamoto and Ludlow, since I am relying partly on memory.
Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, or sees it as a successor step; I judge it distinct but the final vote will show it.
Whether the existing bounds on varying constants, dark matter and gravity are strong enough to be called more than prospective; I would keep the citation off that claim.
Whether B054 will look more mature in one or two years; waiting has a cost if the field consolidates without us.
Whether IceCube's source identification and Spiering's role will be clearer in a year, which is why I keep B029 as a live alternative.
statement.conflict_note: No recusal-level conflict applies to B042. I remain a Fellow of the University of Tokyo (since 2025), where Katori is based, and I have long-running exchanges with Japanese microscopy communities; the link is collegial and not collaborative, and I have no joint work with Katori or Ye. Göran Johansson is a Chalmers Physics colleague, and his stated recusal is for B023, which is not in my configuration. I am personally invested in B056 as a microscopist, so I discount my own opening ranking of it and no longer list it as an alternative.
